target_only_tests.note: Ten target-only tests, translating NO interlock node id and NEVER counted as ported coverage. Two are seam liveness (rulebook rule 5: a seam a refactor stopped routing through would leave every case that replaces it green, because the replacement is simply never reached and the assertions -- which are about refusals -- still hold for the wrong reason). Two are continuo's expression of interlock#71's canary acceptance, which interlock#74 AC4 requires the port to carry rather than drop: interlock states the obligation as "the fencing spawn precondition is wired into the production spawn path", and in a module graph that is asserted, not asserted about -- one case drives every brokenness class through the production entry point and shows the spawner is never invoked, the other pins that src/fencing/spawn.ts imports the renderer and the battery as VALUES rather than as types, so a type-only import (which erases at compile time and would silently unwire the precondition) fails. See DECISIONS.md D-0205. Six more were added by D-0211, and they exist because the property cannot be written in TypeScript: a JSON number's Python spelling is recorded on its container slot (D-0210), the JavaScript literal `1.0` IS `1`, and so a case that built a role body in code carries no spelling into the document and passes against a renderer that has lost it. They serialise the shipped document, patch the numeric literals in as TEXT, read it back through `loadDocument`, drive `FencedSpawner.spawn`, and assert on the BYTES of the written `settings.local.json` and the published fence -- which is where D-0210's repair had stopped one call short. Interlock has no equivalent case because CPython has no equivalent defect: `json.loads` simply keeps the type. The fourth covers `pyDict`'s OTHER rebuild branch -- a sequence of pairs, where the value arrives as element 1 of the pair and its spelling was recorded on the pair rather than on the mapping being built. That branch is not reachable from `FencedSpawner` (a rendered fence always carries an object) but `Fence`, `fenceToJson` and `writeFence` are exported, which is where `pyDict`'s own note says its divergences live; `state.ts` writes the persisted fence through it. The fifth pins the TYPE-NAME half of the same root-slot boundary: a number at a document root has no container to hang a spelling on, so `pyTypeName` guesses, and the guess has to be the DOCUMENT's rule (CPython's syntactic one: no `.`, `e` or `E` makes it an int) rather than the serialiser's `pyNumberKind` -- which classifies values built in code and calls `-0` and anything past 2**53 a float. It also asserts the residue in BOTH directions: an integral float at a root reads `int` here and `float` in CPython, while the same document inside a container reads `float` on both sides. Reached through `FenceLedger.refusals()`, which persists `'<type>' object is not subscriptable`. The sixth covers `FenceLedger.append`, which builds its entry as `{event, at, ...payload}` -- a SPREAD is a rebuild, and it is the only one of the seven on the live spawn path. Without the carry a caller handing it a document-derived payload got the numbers re-spelled by JavaScript (`{"at": 1.0, "big": 9007199254740993}` written as `{"at": 1, "big": 9007199254740992.0}`). The case asserts both halves in one place because they interact: the record is built as ONE map rather than as a carry followed by the `PY_FLOAT` assertion, since `rememberNumberSpellings` REPLACES the record and asserting `at` after carrying would drop everything carried. See DECISIONS.md D-0211.

entries.reason: ADAPTED per D-0206. The source pins that the spawner callback runs OUTSIDE the ledger's cross-process lock: `FenceLedger.transaction` takes an exclusive `fcntl.flock` on a `.lock` sibling, and holding it for the duration of a blocking `claude -p` child would block every other role -- including one trying to record a REFUSAL, which interlock's own comment says must never wait. continuo takes no cross-process lock on any platform (D-0206: Node has no `flock` in core, and a hand-written `O_EXCL` lockfile converts a narrow window into a permanent deadlock on the fail-closed path), so it runs interlock's own `fcntl is None` branch -- the behaviour interlock itself ships on Windows. What the ported case pins is therefore the weaker but still load-bearing half that branch also has, and it pins it exactly as the source does: a second `FencedSpawner` is constructed, spawned and RECORDS its own refusal from INSIDE the first one's spawner callback. If the admission path ever grew a re-entrant in-process lock, or the child were moved inside the transaction, this deadlocks or fails to record, which is the source's failure too. Weaker than the source in the cross-process dimension and no weaker in any other; recorded here rather than left for a later reader to rediscover while wondering why nothing broke.

entries.reason: `monkeypatch.setattr(FencedSpawner, "_write_settings", boom)` patches the CLASS, so an instance built before the patch is affected too -- ordering the source relies on and the port keeps. The port patches `FencedSpawner.prototype.writeSettings` with `patchSeam` (D-0101 exports the method `@internal` for exactly this; `patchSeam` supplies monkeypatch's snapshot-at-patch and LIFO restore rather than a file-level undo, rulebook rule 5). One thing had to be ADDED rather than translated: the thrown error carries an errno-style `code` (`ENOSPC`). Node has no `OSError` class, so `isOSError` in src/fencing/spawn.ts classifies a filesystem failure by the string `code` Node puts on it -- a plain `Error` would escape the publication catch and fail the case with a raw throw instead of exercising the refusal path the source exercises. Every assertion of the source is kept, including `spawner.calls == []`, which is the one that says the child never started (D-0205).

entries.reason: `monkeypatch.setattr(spawn_module, "run_battery", ...)` rebinds a module-level name that `FencedSpawner.spawn` resolves at call time. ESM bindings cannot be rebound from outside and `vi.mock` does not reach an intra-module call, so src/fencing/spawn.ts routes its own call through the exported `spawnSeams` record and the case replaces that entry with `patchSeam` (D-0014, rulebook rule 5). This reproduces Python's late binding rather than working around it: what production calls is what the case replaced. The seam is not decorative -- a target-only liveness case in the same file asserts `FencedSpawner.spawn` reaches `runBattery` through the record, so a refactor that called the function directly would turn red instead of leaving this case green for the wrong reason. Assertions are the source's, unchanged.

inherited_limitations.topic: The ledger's `at`, the fence and the settings file are byte-identical to interlock's; what remains of the number contract is `pyStr` and a scalar-rooted document.
inherited_limitations.status: REPAIRED (D-0210, completed by D-0211). This entry is the measurement, and the residue it names is what is still not carried.
inherited_limitations.detail: This entry previously disclosed a divergence: `FenceLedger.append` records `at` from the injected clock, `time.time()` is a float in Python and JavaScript has one number type, so interlock wrote `"at": 0.0` and continuo wrote `"at": 0`. It was the ONLY field in which a continuo ledger line differed from interlock's for the same inputs. D-0210 repairs it: `pyJsonLoads` now records each number's source spelling on its container slot and `FenceLedger.append` asserts `PY_FLOAT` for the clock's value, which is built in code and has no document behind it. MEASURED rather than argued: interlock's `FencedSpawner.spawn` and continuo's were both driven to an admission over the shipped role document, with the same context paths, the same `python`, the same hook file and the clock pinned to the same value, and all three artefacts -- `fence-worker.json`, `settings.local.json` and `fence-ledger.jsonl` -- compared EQUAL under `cmp` at clocks 0.0, 1700000000.0, 1700000000.5 and 1700000000.125. With the assertion removed the ledger diverges again in exactly one place (`"at": 0` against `"at": 0.0`) and the other two artefacts stay equal, which is the control that says the repair is what closed it. WHAT REMAINS, so the narrower claim above stays true: (1) `pyStr` still renders an integral float as an int, visible only for a role document that spells `role_kind` or `permission_mode` as a number -- no interlock role document does, and the six call sites do not all have a container to take a spelling from (see the note on `pyStr` in src/fencing/pysemantics.ts); (2) a number at the ROOT of a document has no container slot to hang a spelling on, so `pyJsonLoads("1.0")` still dumps as `1` -- every fencing artefact has an object at its root, and the one place a scalar root is reachable is a corrupt ledger line, whose `'float' object is not subscriptable` would read `'int'` here; (3) an integer past 2**53 keeps its exact DIGITS for re-emission but not its exact VALUE, which is still the rounded double. All three are stated in the header of src/fencing/pyjson.ts and pinned, where they are pinnable, by `pyjson.number_documents` in the differential corpus. CORRECTION (D-0211): the measurement above is sound and it was NOT sufficient, and the gap it left is worth recording next to it. It drove the SHIPPED role document, which carries no number in `env`, `permissions`, `sandbox` or `hooks`, so every artefact it compared was byte-equal whether or not the renderer carried the number record past `deepSortKeys` -- and `deepSortKeys` is the last call `settingsPayload` makes before the result becomes `fence.settings`. D-0210 therefore shipped with `settings.local.json` and the persisted fence still diverging for any document that put a number in a settings section (`"env": {"A": 1.0}` rendered `1`), while the artefacts this measurement compared stayed equal. D-0211 carries the record at that site and at a fifth one (`settingsPayload` itself), and pins both with target-only cases that assert on the written bytes; the residue listed above is unchanged. The transferable point is that a differential measurement is bounded by the inputs it is run over, and these inputs could not express the property the repair was about. Residue (2) is narrowed by D-0211 rather than removed: a root number's TYPE NAME is now answered by CPython's syntactic literal rule (no `.`, `e` or `E` is an int) instead of by the serialiser's value-based fallback, which had reported `9007199254740992` and `-0` as `float` where CPython says `int`. What remains at a root is only the integral float -- `1.0` and `1e16` read `int` here, `float` in CPython -- and that is asserted in both directions by a target-only case, together with the control that the same document inside a container answers correctly on both sides.

inherited_limitations.topic: No `.lock` sibling of the ledger file is ever created.
inherited_limitations.detail: interlock's `FenceLedger.transaction` takes an exclusive `fcntl.flock` on `<ledger>.lock`, and degrades to the in-process lock alone where `fcntl` is unavailable -- which is the path it runs in production on Windows. Node has no `flock` in core on any platform, so continuo takes that same degraded branch everywhere (D-0206), and the visible artefact is that the `.lock` file no longer appears beside the ledger. What is lost is exactly one thing: two continuo processes publishing a fence to the SAME path concurrently can interleave their publish-then-record sequences. Each ledger LINE is still atomic (one `O_APPEND` write), within one process nothing is lost at all (every call on the path is synchronous), and publication of the fence file itself is a temp-sibling write plus `rename` and is unaffected. No case in the ported file asserts on the ledger DIRECTORY's contents -- the closest, `test_the_ledger_is_append_only`, reads the ledger FILE -- so no translated assertion depends on the difference. A hand-written `O_EXCL` lockfile was rejected on the record: `flock` is released by the kernel when the holder dies and a lockfile is not, so a SIGKILLed spawner would leave a stale lock blocking every later process, and the operation it blocks is the recording of a refusal, which must never wait. The option to reopen, if multi-process publication to one ledger ever becomes real, is a native binding.

inherited_limitations.topic: The text of a publication failure's refusal reason is Node's error message, not CPython's `str(OSError)`.
inherited_limitations.status: adapted message text (D-0017); the refusal CODE is identical
inherited_limitations.detail: src/fencing/spawn.ts formats a failed publication as `cannot publish fence: ${describe(exc)}` where `describe` is the transcription of CPython's `str(exc)` -- which never prefixes the class name. The message it wraps is the RUNTIME's, so a real ENOSPC reads `ENOSPC: no space left on device, open '<path>'` here where interlock reads `[Errno 28] No space left on device: '<path>'`. D-0017 governs: the refusal reason CODE (`RefusalReason.DOCUMENT_UNREADABLE`) and the sentence the port author writes are parity surface; the operating system's own sentence inside it is not, because no faithful translation of it exists. The two ported cases that reach this path assert on the outcome, the untouched filesystem and the recorded refusal rather than on the wrapped text, so nothing in the suite depends on the difference; a case that matched the message would be matching the platform.
